h: Masons, Z-plans and the castle trail
p: Castle Fraser took a long time to finish. Work began around 1575 under Michael Fraser and carried on for decades, with the castle we see today completed around 1636. It's a classic example of what's known as a Z-plan tower house: a central block with towers at diagonally opposite corners, so defenders could cover every wall. Once you know the shape, walk round the outside and see if you can spot it.

The elaborate top storeys, with their turrets, carved details and fancy roofline, are the work of master masons, and the skill of the craftsmen in this part of Scotland is the reason the area has so many fairy-tale castles. Castle Fraser is one of the stops on Aberdeenshire's Castle Trail, so if you catch the castle bug, there are plenty more to tick off, like Craigievar and Crathes.
Plan on half a day if you're doing the castle, the garden and a walk in the grounds. With younger kids, the trails are a good way to burn off energy after the indoor tour.

Inverurie has its own history to explore. The Bass of Inverurie is a great Norman-era earthwork mound on the edge of town, and the area was the scene of a battle in 1308 when Robert the Bruce defeated the Comyns. Easter Aquhorthies, just outside town, is a well-preserved recumbent stone circle, a type found mainly in this corner of Scotland. And if you fancy a hill walk, Bennachie, with its distinctive Mither Tap peak, is the big local favourite, with views over the whole of the Garioch.
